Tarrant County schools: 16 districts, their money, and every campus

Revenue, federal money, spending and USDA school meals for every independent school district in Tarrant County, Texas, fiscal 2011 through 2025, with meal claims through 2025-26. Three views share one district and one year: the county view puts the 16 districts side by side, the district view follows one district's money from source to spending, and the schools view maps what each campus spends. For the rest of the state, see the Texas explorer.

Federal money by program

School meals and the SNAP connection

USDA pays districts a set amount for every meal served, at a free, reduced-price or paid rate. Under the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP), a school serves everyone free and claims a share of meals at the free rate equal to its identified-student percentage (ISP) × 1.6. The ISP is mostly students matched to SNAP. Districts not on CEP claim students who qualify through SNAP matching or a family application. Either way, fewer SNAP households means fewer meals reimbursed at the free rate.

October claims: students counted free ÷ enrollment. "CEP" marks districts where every school is on the Community Eligibility Provision; "part CEP" where some schools are. A CEP district at 100% has an ISP of at least 62.5%.

Breakfast, lunch and snack claims to the Texas Department of Agriculture, nominal dollars, counting only the months each district claimed in both years so a late or missing month doesn't skew the change.

Spending by function

Shading compares districts within each column (stronger blue = higher). Debt and construction swing with bond programs; recapture is what property-wealthy districts pay the state under Texas school finance.

Enrollment

Fall enrollment indexed to FY2011 = 100. Per-student numbers above divide by this enrollment, so a shrinking district's per-student figures rise even when its budget doesn't.

Spending by function

Each panel has its own scale. The dot marks the selected year; the percentage compares the last year shown with the first.

School meals and the SNAP connection

USDA pays a district a set amount for every meal served, at a free, reduced-price or paid rate. Under the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP) a school serves everyone free and claims a share of meals at the free rate equal to its identified-student percentage (ISP) × 1.6. The ISP is mostly students directly certified through SNAP, TANF, foster care, homeless or migrant records instead of a paper application. Fewer SNAP households means fewer directly certified students, and that lowers the reimbursement for the same meal.

USDA child-nutrition revenue (actuals)

From the district's food-service fund in TEA PEIMS, nominal dollars. Commodities are USDA Foods valued at cost. Pandemic-era summer and year-round meals (Seamless Summer Option) are booked as breakfast and lunch.

Meals claimed by school year

Texas Department of Agriculture reimbursement claims. In 2020-21 most meals were served under the Seamless Summer Option, so regular school-year claims are small or missing.

Share of students claimed at the free rate

October claims: students counted free ÷ enrollment. 2020-21 and 2021-22 are left out because USDA waivers let every school serve free meals. Dashed line: the ISP implied by that share (÷ 1.6) in years when every school was on CEP; at a 100% free share the ISP is at least 62.5%.

Monthly USDA reimbursement: 2024-25 vs 2025-26

School-year National School Lunch and School Breakfast claims only (no summer or after-school supper).

Budgeted food-service spending (adopted budgets)

Function 35 across official funds. FY2026 includes the district's PEIMS food-service budget (fund 240), which ran about $12 million above that fund's revenue.

    All schools

    Sources and method

    • Revenue and spending FY2011–FY2025: Texas Education Agency, PEIMS district actual financial data (audited, every fund, function, object and organization code), for TEA district numbers 220901–220920. "All funds" means the General Fund, food service, federal and state/local grant funds, Debt Service and Capital Projects. Internal-service and fiduciary funds are left out so money isn't counted twice. Bond proceeds, refundings and transfers between funds aren't revenue; in the money-flow chart they show up only as the balancing node "Fund balance, bonds & transfers". Charter schools in the county aren't included.
    • Federal categories follow TEA fund codes: 211/276 Title I; 224–226 IDEA-B; 266 (FY2020+), 277, 279, 281–285 COVID relief; 266 (FY2011) and 283–287 (FY2011–13) the 2009 stimulus and Education Jobs; General Fund objects 5931/5932 Medicaid. USDA child nutrition is federal revenue in the food-service fund, which districts book as enterprise fund 701, special revenue fund 240, General Fund-group fund 101 (Everman) or summer-feeding fund 242 (pandemic meals in Arlington and Hurst-Euless-Bedford).
    • School spending: the same TEA file. Every expenditure carries an organization code; codes 001–699 are campuses and 7xx–999 are district-wide units. School spending is everything coded to a campus in the General Fund, special revenue (federal and state grant) funds and food service. Debt service, construction and internal-service funds are left out. District-wide costs (central administration, most transportation and maintenance, technology, some special-education services) aren't assigned to schools, so school figures understate the full cost of educating a student; the schools view shows the district-wide amount per student. School-level funding source: General Fund and state/local grants are "state & local"; Title I, IDEA, COVID relief and other federal funds as above; food-service funds are child nutrition. School-level function groups: instruction (11, 95); curriculum, libraries and campus leadership (12, 13, 21, 23); counseling, health and social work (31–33); food service (35); everything else. School amounts are stored rounded to $1,000.
    • Fort Worth ISD adopted budgets FY2023–FY2027: the district's budget documents: Budget Books 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25 (All Funds table), and the 2024-25 and 2026-27 Adopted Budget postings. The posted 2025-26 adopted budget covers only the General Fund, so that year's Food Service and Debt Service figures come from the district's PEIMS budget submission to TEA. The 2026-27 posting has no fund split. Budgets cover only the three funds Texas requires a board to adopt, so most federal grants aren't in them. Adopted budgets for the other 15 districts haven't been transcribed.
    • School meals: Texas Department of Agriculture open data on data.texas.gov: School Nutrition Programs meal reimbursement (one row per school per month, program years 2015-16 to 2025-26), Seamless Summer Option and CACFP at-risk reimbursement, contracting entities 01017–01032. Claim site ids match TEA campus numbers. Carroll ISD doesn't take part in the National School Lunch Program, so it has no claims and almost no USDA revenue. Reimbursement comparisons between 2024-25 and 2025-26 count only the months claimed in both years.
    • School directory: NCES Common Core of Data, school years 2010-11 to 2023-24 via the Urban Institute Education Data API, and 2024-25 from NCES EDGE: coordinates, address, grades, enrollment, free/reduced-price eligible counts and teachers. Schools are linked to TEA campus numbers through the state school id. School per-student figures divide by that year's NCES enrollment.
    • District enrollment: TEA Summarized PEIMS Actual Financial Data, fall survey enrollment. For Fort Worth's FY2026 and FY2027 budgets, per-student values use the enrollment implied by the district's own per-pupil figures.
    • Map: base map is Esri's Light and Dark Gray Canvas (Esri, TomTom, Garmin, © OpenStreetMap contributors and the GIS user community); drawn with Leaflet. District boundaries from the U.S. Census Bureau (TIGERweb unified school districts). The map needs an internet connection; everything else on the page works offline.
    • Inflation: CPI-U (not seasonally adjusted) from FRED, averaged July–June to match the fiscal year. FY2027 uses July–September 2026 only.
    • Fiscal years run July 1 to June 30 and are named for the year they end, so FY2025 is the 2024-25 school year. District boundaries don't follow city or county lines: Northwest, Aledo, Burleson and others reach into Tarrant County but are based in neighboring counties and aren't shown. Rebuild with build/fetch.sh and build/build_data.py.
    • This page merges three earlier ones, which are kept with their original prompts: the Fort Worth ISD budget explorer, the Tarrant County ISD comparison and the Fort Worth area schools map.
